questions.stem: Determine the enzyme that is competitively inhibited by statin drugs.
questions.why: Statins are structural analogs of HMG-CoA. They competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis.

questions.stem: Which of these enzymes deactivates HMG-CoA Reductase?
questions.why: AMPK acts as a cellular energy sensor. When cellular energy is low, it phosphorylates HMG-CoA reductase, which inactivates the enzyme.

questions.stem: Which enzyme activates AMP activated kinase?
questions.why: Upstream kinases (such as LKB1 or CaMKKβ) phosphorylate AMPK to activate it.

questions.stem: cAMP indirectly deactivates HMG-CoA Reductase, through which protein is this effect mediated?
questions.why: Glucagon/epinephrine increases cAMP, which activates PKA. PKA initiates a cascade that keeps HMG-CoA reductase phosphorylated and inactive.

questions.stem: The rate-limiting step in fatty acid synthesis is:

options.label: C
options.text: formation of malonyl-CoA from malonate and coenzyme A.

options.label: D
options.text: the reaction catalyzed by acetyl-CoA carboxylase.

options.label: E
options.text: the reduction of the acetoacetyl group to a β-hydroxybutyryl group

questions.why: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) catalyzes the committed, rate-limiting step of fatty acid synthesis.

questions.stem: The biosynthesis of triacylglycerols from acetate occurs mainly in:

options.label: B
options.text: humans after ingestion of excess carbohydrate.

questions.why: Excess dietary carbohydrates are converted to acetyl-CoA and then to triacylglycerols for storage in humans.

questions.stem: Which of these statements about triacylglycerol synthesis is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Humans can store more energy in glycogen than in triacylglycerols.

options.label: B
options.text: Insulin stimulates conversion of dietary carbohydrate into triacylglycerols.

options.label: C
options.text: It is not a hormone-sensitive process.

options.label: D
options.text: Mammals are unable to convert carbohydrates into triacylglycerols.

options.label: E
options.text: Phosphatidate is not on the pathway of triacylglycerol synthesis.

questions.why: Insulin promotes lipogenesis (converting carbs to fat) and inhibits lipolysis.

questions.stem: A strategy that is not employed in the synthesis of phospholipids is:

options.label: D
options.text: exchange of free alcohol with head group alcohol of phospholipid.

options.label: E
options.text: remodeling of head group alcohols by chemical modification

questions.why: Phospholipid synthesis involves CDP-activated intermediates, but not condensation of two CDP-linked molecules.

questions.stem: The major source of cholesterol in arterial smooth muscle cells is from:
questions.why: LDL delivers cholesterol to peripheral tissues via receptor-mediated endocytosis.

questions.stem: Endogenous triglycerides in plasma is maximally bound to:
questions.why: VLDL transports endogenously synthesized triglycerides from the liver.

questions.stem: The precursor of cholesterol synthesis is:
questions.why: All 27 carbons of cholesterol are derived from acetyl-CoA.

questions.stem: All are derived of cholesterol except:
questions.why: Cholecystokinin is a peptide hormone from the duodenum, made from amino acids. Bile acids (chenodeoxycholic and glycocholic acid), steroid hormones (testosterone) and vitamin D are all made from cholesterol.

questions.stem: Determine the lipoprotein that best detect Lipid profile of a non-fasting patient:
questions.why: Non-fasting blood primarily reflects the presence of dietary chylomicrons.

questions.stem: Clinically, bile acids are important in:

options.label: B
options.text: enhancing the formation of atherogenic plaques

options.label: C
options.text: inhibition of intestinal absorption of fat soluble vitamins

questions.why: Converting cholesterol to bile acids and excreting them in faeces is the body's main route for getting rid of excess cholesterol (sterol). Bile acids emulsify fats; they do not precipitate them, they do not promote plaques, they are needed FOR fat-soluble vitamin absorption, and they do not cause fatty liver.

questions.stem: A person with a type IIA hyperlipoproteinemia had a blood cholesterol level of 360 mg/dL and blood triglyceride levels of 140 mg/dL. This person most likely has:

options.label: A
options.text: an increased ability to produce VLDL

options.label: B
options.text: a decreased ability for receptor-mediated endocytosis of LDL

options.label: C
options.text: an elevation of HDL in the blood

options.label: D
options.text: a decreased ability to convert VLDL to IDL

questions.why: Type IIA is familial hypercholesterolemia, typically due to defective LDL receptors, preventing LDL clearance.

questions.stem: A person with a low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor deficiency was treated with lovastatin. As a consequence of the action of this drug, the person should have:

options.label: A
options.text: fewer LDL receptors in cell membranes

questions.why: Statins lower intracellular cholesterol, causing cells to upregulate LDL receptors, which clears LDL from the blood.

questions.stem: Arrange the following lipoproteins in increasing order of density:
questions.why: Density rises as the lipid:protein ratio falls: chylomicrons < VLDL < IDL < LDL < HDL. None of the listed sequences follows that order.

questions.stem:
During fatty acid synthesis, the growing acyl chain is covalently attached to which of the following? Key:
I. NADPH
II. β-keto-acyl:ACP reductase
III. enoyl-ACP reductase
IV. ACP1 and ACP2
V. ACP-acyl transferase
questions.why: The growing chain is held as a thioester on the acyl carrier protein arms (the pantetheinyl -SH of ACP and the cysteinyl -SH of the condensing enzyme, called ACP1 and ACP2 in this course). NADPH and the reductases act on the chain but do not carry it.

questions.stem: Transfers Acetyl group from CoA to cysteinyl-S on ACP.
questions.why: Acetyl-CoA: ACP transacylase transfers the acetyl group from Coenzyme A to the active site of the ACP.

questions.stem: Transfers Malonyl group from CoA to pantetheinyl-S on ACP.
questions.why: Malonyl-CoA: ACP transacylase transfers the malonyl group to the phosphopantetheine arm of the ACP.

questions.stem: In this reaction CO2 departs from malonylCoA reducing ACP. Which enzyme catalyzes this?
questions.why: The condensation reaction joins the acetyl and malonyl groups, decarboxylating the malonyl group to release CO2. This is catalyzed by Keto Acyl: ACP synthase.

questions.stem:
Reduction of the keto group to an alcohol requires: Key:
I. NADPH
II. β-keto-acyl:ACP reductase
III. enoyl-ACP reductase
IV. ACP1 and ACP2
V. ACP-acyl transferase
questions.why: The enzyme β-keto-Acyl: ACP reductase (II) reduces the keto group to a hydroxyl group, and it requires NADPH (I).

questions.stem:
The enoyl group is reduced to a saturated group by: Key:
I. NADPH
II. β-keto-acyl:ACP reductase
III. enoyl-ACP reductase
IV. ACP1 and ACP2
V. ACP-acyl transferase
questions.why: Enoyl-ACP reductase (III) reduces the double bond to a single bond, utilizing NADPH (I).

questions.stem: Most potent reducing agent in fatty acid synthesis:
questions.why: NADPH provides the reducing power for the two reduction steps in fatty acid synthesis.

questions.stem: What constitutes the substrate-carrying arm of the synthase complex:
questions.why: The Acyl Carrier Protein (ACP) holds the growing fatty acid chain during synthesis.

questions.stem: Deficiency of lipoprotein lipase may not give rise to the following clinical manifestation:
questions.why: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency causes hypertriglyceridemia, hepatosplenomegaly, and xanthomas, but not muscular dystrophy.

questions.stem: Type III hyperlipidemia is caused by a deficiency in apoprotein E. Analysis of the serum of patient with this disorder would exhibit which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: An absence of chylomicrons after eating

options.label: B
options.text: Normal levels of VLDL after eating

questions.why: ApoE is needed for the liver to take up chylomicron remnants and IDL. Without it these remnants accumulate, so both triglycerides and cholesterol are raised (type III, dysbetalipoproteinaemia).

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true of the fatty acid elongation system of vertebrate cells?

options.label: A
options.text: It involves the same four-step sequence seen in the fatty acid synthase complex.

options.label: B
options.text: It is located in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum.

options.label: C
options.text: It produces stearoyl-CoA by the extension of palmitoyl-CoA.

options.label: D
options.text: It uses malonyl-CoA as a substrate.

options.label: E
options.text: The immediate precursor of the added carbons is acetyl-CoA.

questions.why: The immediate precursor of added carbons is malonyl-CoA, not acetyl-CoA.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true of the differences between fatty acid synthesis and fatty acid β-oxidation?

options.label: A
options.text: A thioester derivative of crotonic acid (trans-2-butenoic acid) is an intermediate in the synthetic path, but not in the degradative path.

options.label: B
options.text: A thioester derivative of D-β-hydroxybutyrate is an intermediate in the synthetic path, not in the degradative path.

options.label: C
options.text: Fatty acid synthesis uses NADPH, whereas β-oxidation produces NADH and FADH2.

options.label: D
options.text: Fatty acid degradation is catalysed by cytosolic enzymes; fatty acid synthesis by mitochondrial enzymes.

options.label: E
options.text: The condensation of two acetyl-CoA molecules in a crude extract is faster in bicarbonate buffer than in phosphate buffer at the same pH.

questions.why: It is the reverse: fatty acid synthesis is cytosolic and β-oxidation is mitochondrial. The other statements are true (synthesis uses the D-isomer and NADPH; bicarbonate is needed for acetyl-CoA carboxylase).

questions.stem: A healthy 70-year-old man is told to fast for 12 hours before his plasma lipids are measured, but he eats a large breakfast 3 hours before the blood draw. Which change is most likely?
questions.why: Dietary fat is carried from the gut as chylomicrons, so a recent meal sharply raises chylomicrons and plasma triglycerides. LDL- and HDL-cholesterol change very little after one meal, which is why triglycerides need a fasting sample.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Friedewald equation is considered fairly accurate and widely employed.
Reason: some factors that could cause deviations in the Friedewald equation are unaccounted for using this calculation.
questions.why: Both are true. The Friedewald equation (LDL = TC − HDL − TG/5 in mg/dL) is widely used because it is simple and cheap, and it does ignore factors (e.g. TG above about 4.5 mmol/L, chylomicrons) that make it inaccurate. But those limitations do not explain why it is considered accurate, so the reason is not the explanation.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Hypertriglyceridemia may lead to Pancreatitis.
Reason: excessively elevated levels of chylomicrons from diet can cause occlusion of the capillaries leading to ischaemia and local acidaemia which can expose triglycerides to pancreatic lipases whose effect is the degradation of triglycerides to free fatty acids, causing to cytotoxic injury.
questions.why: Both statements are true. High chylomicrons cause capillary occlusion, leading to ischemia and acidosis, which activates pancreatic lipases to release toxic free fatty acids.

questions.stem: Enzymes that catalyze the synthesis of long chain fatty acids in vertebrate cells:

options.label: C
options.text: are localized in the mitochondrial matrix.

options.label: D
options.text: are part of a single polypeptide chain containing several distinct enzyme activities.

options.label: E
options.text: have none of the characteristics above.

questions.why: In vertebrates, fatty acid synthase is a multifunctional megaprotein.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true of the fatty acid synthasis and the fatty acid β-oxidation systems?

options.label: A
options.text: A derivative of the vitamin pantothenic acid is involved.

options.label: C
options.text: Double bonds are oxidized or reduced by pyridine nucleotide coenzymes.

options.label: D
options.text: The processes occur in different cellular compartments.

options.label: E
options.text: The processes occur in the mitochondrial matrix.

questions.why: Fatty acid synthesis occurs in the cytosol; only beta-oxidation occurs in the mitochondria.

questions.stem: HMG CoA reductase is inhibited by:
questions.why: Lovastatin is a statin, which competitively inhibits HMG-CoA reductase.

questions.stem: Atherosclerosis can be managed by the following drug treatment:
questions.why: Simvastatin, a statin, inhibits HMG-CoA reductase and is the main drug for lowering LDL in atherosclerosis. Niacin works only at high doses, and diet or surgery are not drug treatments.

questions.stem: Atherosclerotic plaques development cannot be accelerated under the following pathological conditions:

options.label: A
options.text: The consumption of high fat diets

questions.why: HDL is cardioprotective and prevents plaque formation.

questions.stem: The clinical importance of apolipoproteins:

options.label: A
options.text: Solubilization of lipids in the gut

options.label: C
options.text: Can inactivate some lipid metabolic enzymes

options.label: D
options.text: Prevents the cholestasis of bile salts

questions.why: ApoB-100 and ApoE act as ligands for receptors.

questions.stem: Which apoprotein is the main structural protein of VLDL?
questions.why: Apo B-100 is the structural protein of VLDL (and IDL and LDL) and the ligand for the LDL receptor. Apo B-48 belongs to chylomicrons and Apo A-I to HDL; VLDL picks up C-II and E from HDL, but they are not its structural protein.

questions.stem: The most important long-term clinical consequence of persistently raised plasma VLDL is:
questions.why: VLDL and its remnants are atherogenic, so persistently high VLDL promotes atherosclerosis. Hepatosplenomegaly and abdominal pain (pancreatitis) are features of very high chylomicrons, and lipoprotein lipase deficiency is a cause, not a consequence.

questions.stem: Lipidoses:

options.label: A
options.text: are acquired diseases of catabolism of lipids

options.label: B
options.text: there is deficiency of the respective lipid substrate in the nervous system and/or peripheral tissues

options.label: C
options.text: there is accumulation of lipid substrate in the stomach resulting in obesity

options.label: D
options.text: the clinical chemical diagnosis can be accomplished by demonstration of the enzyme defect

options.label: E
options.text: the clinical chemical diagnosis cannot be accomplished by the demonstration of substrate accumulation in body fluids

questions.why: Lipidoses (lipid storage diseases) are diagnosed by demonstrating the specific enzyme defect.

questions.stem: Mechanism of action of drugs regulating Familial hypercholestolaemia:

options.label: A
options.text: Cholestyramine: combines with bile acids and prevent cholesterol reabsorption

options.label: B
options.text: Cholestyramine: combines with lipoprotein lipase and prevent cholesterol reabsorption

options.label: C
options.text: Small doses of niacin prevent cholesterol absorption

options.label: D
options.text: Large doses of niacin prevent cholesterol excretion

questions.why: Cholestyramine is a bile acid sequestrant.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman has a mild heart attack and is placed on diet and statin therapy. What will be the most likely result of this therapy?
questions.why: Statins lower LDL levels, reducing the risk of further cardiovascular events.

questions.stem: Type I hyperlipidemia may be caused by a deficiency of apoprotein C-II. What would be exhibited by analysis of the serum of patients with this disorder?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher than normal levels of VLDL after eating

questions.why: ApoC-II is required for lipoprotein lipase to clear chylomicrons and VLDL, so a deficiency leads to elevated triglycerides.

questions.stem: Lipoprotein particle metabolism can occur:

options.label: A
options.text: via the exogenous or endogenous pathway,

options.label: B
options.text: Independent of the source of origin.

questions.why: Lipoproteins are metabolized via exogenous (dietary) and endogenous (hepatic) pathways.

questions.stem: Lipoproteins are characterized based on their various proportions which determine their by their density. Which one of the following sequences places the lipoproteins in the order of most dense to least dense?
questions.why: The correct order from most dense to least dense is HDL > LDL > VLDL > Chylomicrons.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Atherosclerosis is a disease where capillary walls become less elastic and thicker.
Reason: fatty materials accumulate beneath the outer lining of the capillary wall.
questions.why: Both are false. Atherosclerosis affects arteries (not capillaries), and lipid accumulates beneath the INNER lining (intima), not the outer lining.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Bile salts are not essential to lipid metabolism.
Reason: bile salts can be produced by the body.
questions.why: The assertion is false; bile salts are essential for emulsifying lipids. The reason is true.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase may not be the most desirable method for controlling cholesterol levels.
Reason: mevalonate is needed for the synthesis of important molecules such as acetyl CoA.
questions.why: The assertion is true. The reason is false: mevalonate is a precursor for cholesterol, CoQ10, and dolichol, but not acetyl CoA.

questions.stem: Kofi, a 35-year-old, has been diagnosed with severe hypercholesterolaemia. Which of the following plasma cholesterol levels would indicate this condition?

options.label: E
options.text: Patient may not suffer from heart attack

questions.why: A total plasma cholesterol greater than 7.0 mmol/L is a definitive indicator of severe hypercholesterolemia.

questions.stem: Which finding would cause impaired emulsification of dietary fat?

options.label: E
options.text: Patient may not suffer from heart attack

questions.why: Bile salts emulsify dietary fat into small droplets for pancreatic lipase. Low bile salts and acids therefore impair emulsification and fat absorption.

questions.stem: Low emulsification may lead to one of these clinical presentations:

options.label: E
options.text: Patient may not suffer from heart attack

questions.why: Emulsification is the physical breakdown of fat globules. If this doesn't happen, the fat remains too large for pancreatic lipase to act on, resulting in fat malabsorption.

questions.stem: Which clinical presentation is contrary to hypercholesterolaemia?

options.label: E
options.text: Patient may not suffer from heart attack

questions.why: Hypercholesterolemia directly causes atherosclerosis, which drastically increases the risk of heart attacks. Therefore, stating the patient 'may not suffer a heart attack' is contrary to the disease.

questions.stem: Besides congenital enzyme deficiency, which of these conditions could result in hypocholesterolaemia?

options.label: E
options.text: Patient may not suffer from heart attack

questions.why: If the body cannot absorb dietary fats/cholesterol from the gut, plasma cholesterol levels will drop significantly.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a source of cholesterol?
questions.why: Carrots are plant-based and do not contain cholesterol (plants do not synthesize cholesterol).

questions.stem: Which of the following is derived from a sterol?
questions.why: Bile salts are made from cholesterol, a sterol. Gangliosides are sphingolipids, geraniol is an isoprenoid on the path TO sterols, phosphatidylglycerol is a glycerophospholipid, and prostaglandins are eicosanoids from arachidonic acid.

questions.stem: Mechanism of action of statins in the treatment of hypercholesterolaemia:
questions.why: Statins competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis. Lower liver cholesterol then upregulates LDL receptors, which clears LDL from the blood.

questions.stem: Antioxidant is:

options.label: A
options.text: a substance which catalyzes the formation of free radicals

options.label: B
options.text: a substance which neutralizes the formation of free radicals

questions.why: Antioxidants neutralize or scavenge free radicals, preventing them from causing cellular damage.

questions.stem: The antioxidant properties of a substance depends on:

options.label: A
options.text: The molecular structure of the substance

options.label: B
options.text: The redox state of the surrounding environment

options.label: C
options.text: Presence of oxygen and transition metal ions

questions.why: An antioxidant's effectiveness is influenced by its chemical structure, the local redox environment, and the presence of metals.

questions.stem: The free radical causes damage to:
questions.why: Free radicals are highly reactive and can damage all major macromolecules in the cell.

questions.stem: Dietary carotenoids are efficient quenchers of singlet oxygen:

options.label: A
options.text: Due to their wide distribution in nature

options.label: B
options.text: Due to their highly conjugated double-bond system

options.label: C
options.text: Due to the presence of methyl group in their structure

questions.why: The long conjugated double-bond system allows carotenoids to absorb the excess energy from singlet oxygen.

questions.stem: How are anti-oxidants believed to be helpful to our bodies?

options.label: A
options.text: they antagonistically bind to oxygen molecules, thus preventing aerobic pathways

options.label: B
options.text: they enhance free-radical formation, thus increasing the efficiency of cellular processes

options.label: C
options.text: they 'quench' the reactivity of reactive oxygen species, thus preventing their detrimental interactions

options.label: D
options.text: they complex with vitamins in our bodies to produce reactive oxygen species

questions.why: Antioxidants scavenge or quench ROS, preventing them from reacting with and damaging cellular components.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not true? The Fenton reaction:

options.label: A
options.text: results in the formation of hydroxyl radicals

options.label: B
options.text: involves redox cycling of Fe(III) to Fe(II) and vice versa

options.label: C
options.text: results in electrons being transferred from superoxide anions to hydrogen peroxide

questions.why: The Fenton reaction generates highly toxic hydroxyl radicals; it does not protect against oxidative stress.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not true? The superoxide anion is:

options.label: B
options.text: a free radical reactive oxygen species

options.label: C
options.text: converted to water by superoxide dismutase

options.label: D
options.text: able to react with hydrogen peroxide producing hydroxyl radicals

questions.why: SOD converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), not water.

questions.stem: It is untrue that with respect to reactive oxygen species:

options.label: A
options.text: the superoxide anion is a free radical

options.label: B
options.text: hydrogen peroxide is a free radical

options.label: C
options.text: the hydroxyl radical is extremely reactive

questions.why: Hydrogen peroxide is a reactive oxygen species but not a free radical, because it has no unpaired electron. Superoxide is a radical, the hydroxyl radical is the most reactive species known in biology, and H2O2 crosses membranes because it is lipid soluble.

questions.stem: A young boy has fever for which Antimalarial drugs have been administered. Following this he passed black coloured Urine, which improved after four days. Which condition should be considered as a Likely possibility?
questions.why: Antimalarials cause oxidative stress; in G6PD deficiency, this leads to hemolysis (black urine).

questions.stem: What enzyme, or combination of enzymes, protects cells against superoxide generated in oxidation reactions?
questions.why: SOD converts superoxide to H2O2, and catalase then converts the H2O2 into water and oxygen.

questions.stem: All of the following enzymes may contribute in generating free oxygen radicals within neutrophils for killing intracellular bacteria except?
questions.why: Glutathione peroxidase detoxifies peroxides; it does not generate radicals.

questions.stem: The glutathione cycle is the conversion of oxidized glutathione to reduced glutathione in the presence of NADPH. Which of the following enzyme catalyzes this reaction?
questions.why: Glutathione reductase uses NADPH to reduce oxidized glutathione (GSSG) back to reduced glutathione (GSH).

questions.stem: Free radicals can be inactivated by the following enzymes EXCEPT:
questions.why: Myeloperoxidase generates hypochlorous acid (a strong oxidant).

questions.stem: Which of the following statement is not true with respect to detoxification of ROS?

options.label: A
options.text: superoxide dismutase (SOD) is found in both mitochondria and cytoplasm

options.label: B
options.text: SOD catalyzes the conversion of superoxide anions to hydrogen peroxide

options.label: C
options.text: catalase converts hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen

options.label: D
options.text: glutathione catalyzes the conversion of hydrogen peroxide to water

questions.why: It is the enzyme glutathione peroxidase that catalyzes this, not glutathione itself.

questions.stem: Which of the following statement is not true with respect to oxidative stress?

options.label: B
options.text: mitochondria constantly release hydrogen peroxide into the cytoplasm of cells

options.label: C
options.text: cells possess redox sensors such as KEAP1/Nrf2

options.label: D
options.text: DNA is resistant to oxidative damage

questions.why: DNA is highly susceptible to oxidative damage.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most reactive free radical in the body?
questions.why: The hydroxyl radical (OH•) is the most reactive radical in biology; it reacts almost instantly with whatever molecule is next to it. Superoxide (O2•−) is less reactive, and H2O2 is not a radical.

questions.stem: True or false: Different anti-oxidants are needed to protect oxidative stress and cell injury.
questions.why: Antioxidants have different solubilities and target different radicals.

questions.stem: True or false: Failure to find lipid peroxidation does not rule out the occurrence of oxidative stress.
questions.why: Oxidative stress can damage DNA and proteins directly without necessarily causing lipid peroxidation.

questions.stem: True or false: A chain-breaking antioxidant such as Vit. E is a therapeutic event.
questions.why: Chain-breaking antioxidants stop the propagation of lipid peroxidation.

questions.stem: True or false: Oncogenesis can occur during lipid peroxidation.
questions.why: Byproducts of lipid peroxidation (like malondialdehyde) are mutagenic and can initiate cancer.

questions.stem: True or false: Ascorbic acid, zinc and Selenium are recommended supplementary antioxidant therapies.
questions.why: Vitamin C is a direct antioxidant; Zinc and Selenium are essential cofactors for antioxidant enzymes.

questions.stem: True or false: DNA damage can result in the generation of reactive oxidative species.
questions.why: DNA damage can trigger cellular stress pathways that lead to mitochondrial dysfunction and more ROS.

questions.stem:
In the light of Reactive Oxidative Species (ROS):
I. ROS are generated as a consequence to the body's own natural processes.
II. Disease processes can generate reactive radicals in presence of hydrogen peroxide.
III. ROS can be generated consequent to tissue damage.
questions.why: Normal metabolism produces ROS, diseases produce them, and tissue damage generates them.

questions.stem:
Considering the eukaryotic cell, any of these cellular organelles can be a source of ROS:
I. Nucleus
II. Mitochondria
III. Cytoplasm
questions.why: Mitochondria are the primary source. The nucleus and cytoplasm also produce ROS.

questions.stem:
The following are rich sources of anti-oxidants:
I. coffee
II. almond nuts
III. mushrooms
questions.why: Coffee (polyphenols), almonds (Vitamin E), and mushrooms (ergothioneine) are all excellent sources.

questions.stem:
The following are generally extracellular anti-oxidant defences:
I. Lactoferrin
II. Ceruloplasmin
III. Haptoglobin
questions.why: All three are extracellular proteins that prevent oxidative damage in the blood.

questions.stem:
The following anti-oxidants remove free radicals by directly reacting with them catalytically:
I. GSH
II. Vit. C
III. Urate
questions.why: Glutathione and Vitamin C can act catalytically (they are regenerated). Urate acts stoichiometrically.

questions.stem: Which of the following is likely to be associated with lipid peroxidation?

options.label: A
options.text: Intermittent generation of OH* can combine with O2 to give only alkoxyl radicals

options.label: B
options.text: Hydroxyl radicals during lipid peroxidation can generate peroxyl moieties to give rise to alkoxyl radicals

options.label: C
options.text: Free radicals reactions during lipid peroxidation can combine with nearby saturated fatty acids

options.label: D
options.text: Hydroxyl radicals during lipid peroxidation can combine with O2 to give peroxyl radicals capable of abstracting H* and forming peroxides

questions.why: The mechanism is: OH* attacks a polyunsaturated fatty acid to form a lipid radical. This radical reacts with O2 to form a lipid peroxyl radical.

questions.stem: True or false: Protein degradation consequent to free radical attack occurs at the molecular level.
questions.why: Free radicals cause oxidative damage to proteins, marking them for degradation by the proteasome.

questions.stem:
Which of the following antioxidants are generated internally?
I. GSH
II. Urate
III. Vitamin C
questions.why: The body synthesizes glutathione (GSH) and uric acid (urate) internally. Vitamin C must be obtained from the diet.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not true? Paraquat is:

options.label: C
options.text: able to receive electrons from superoxide anions

options.label: D
options.text: cytotoxic to type I and II pneumocytes

options.label: E
options.text: catalyzes the flow of electrons from NADPH/NADH to oxygen

questions.why: Paraquat receives electrons from NADPH/NADH and transfers them to oxygen to form superoxide.

questions.stem: Free radicals are capable of independent existence and have a single unpaired electron. Which of the following best describes a reactive oxygen species (ROS)?

options.label: A
options.text: Free radicals capable of interacting with oxygen

options.label: B
options.text: Free radicals that cannot interact with oxygen

options.label: C
options.text: Oxygen compounds that are reactive free radicals

options.label: D
options.text: Oxygen compounds that can only react with free radicals

options.label: E
options.text: Oxygen compounds that cannot react with free radicals

questions.why: ROS includes oxygen compounds that are reactive free radicals (and non-radical derivatives like H2O2).

questions.stem:
The following are Eukaryotic cellular sources of Free radicals;
I. Lysosomes
II. Cell membranes
III. Mitochondria
questions.why: Free radicals are generated in mitochondria (electron transport chain), lysosomes and phagosomes, and at cell membranes (NADPH oxidase, lipoxygenases), so all three are sources.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements; select the correct one(s):
I. Oxidative protein damage occurs during X-ray crystallography.
II. Oxidative protein damage consequent to a free radical attack can impair the functioning of receptors.
III. Oxidative protein damage consequent to a free radical attack cannot impair the activities of antibodies.
questions.why: X-rays generate ROS which damage proteins (i). Free radicals damage receptor proteins (ii). Antibodies are proteins and can be damaged (iii is false).

questions.stem:
The following are rich sources of anti-oxidants:
I. coffee
II. almond nuts
III. mushrooms
questions.why: Coffee, almonds, and mushrooms are all excellent dietary sources of antioxidants.

questions.stem:
The following are generally intracellular anti-oxidant defences:
I. Urate
II. Alpha-tocopherol
III. Transferrin
questions.why: Alpha-tocopherol (Vitamin E) is a major lipid-soluble intracellular antioxidant. Urate and Transferrin are extracellular.

questions.stem: Which of the following is associated with lipid peroxidation?

options.label: A
options.text: Initial OH attack can generate free radicals to combine with O2 to give only alkoxyl radicals.

options.label: B
options.text: Initial OH attack can generate peroxyls moieties to give alkoxyl radicals.

questions.why: The initial hydroxyl radical attack forms a lipid radical, which reacts with O2 to form a peroxyl radical. This peroxyl radical then abstracts a hydrogen from another lipid to form a lipid hydroperoxide and a new alkoxyl radical.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Antioxidants like selenium are crucial to the body antioxidant defense system.
Reason: Antioxidants like selenium have reversible oxidative states.
questions.why: Both are true. However, selenium works by being incorporated into enzymes (like glutathione peroxidase), not just by its own reversible oxidation.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Foods like carrot, oranges, Water melon are rich in vitamins and antioxidants.
Reason: they are fruits.
questions.why: The assertion is true: carrots, oranges and watermelon are rich in vitamins and antioxidants (carotenoids, vitamin C). The reason is false: a carrot is a root vegetable, not a fruit, and being a fruit is not what makes a food rich in antioxidants.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Free radicals, which are harmful to the body, can form from events such as aging.
Reason: Free radicals are also by products of the body's natural processes.
questions.why: Both true. Aging is associated with free radical formation, which are generated as byproducts of normal metabolism.

ROS Activity at Cellular Levels

questions.stem: y-glutamylcysteine is a precursor to glutathione. Glutathione synthesized helps prevent:
questions.why: Glutathione is a major antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative damage caused by free radicals.

questions.stem: When Free Radicals surmounts the counteract effect of antioxidants; it results to:
questions.why: Oxidative stress is defined as an imbalance where the production of free radicals exceeds the body's antioxidant defense capacity.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a source of free radicals:
questions.why: All listed options (p450 enzymes, macrophages, alloxan, and lipid peroxidation) are well-known sources or generators of free radicals in the body.

questions.stem: What amino acids are found in protein?
questions.why: Almost all naturally occurring amino acids incorporated into biological proteins are L-α-amino acids.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an acidic/basic amino acid?
questions.why: Serine is a polar uncharged amino acid. Arginine and Lysine are basic; Glutamate is acidic.

questions.stem: What form of bond holds the amino acid sequence of proteins?
questions.why: The primary structure (sequence) of a protein is held together by peptide bonds.

questions.stem: The secondary structure of amino Acids peptides are held by which form of bond?
questions.why: Secondary structures (like α-helices and β-pleated sheets) are stabilized by hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not involved in cystinuria?
questions.why: Cystinuria is a defect of the renal and intestinal transporter for cystine and the dibasic amino acids: cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine (COLA). Tryptophan is not involved (its transport defect is Hartnup disease).

questions.stem: The Nitrogen in urea Cycle is derived from;
questions.why: The urea cycle incorporates nitrogen from ammonia via carbamoyl phosphate, and from aspartate.

questions.stem: What is the role of N-acetyl glutamate in ureogenesis?
questions.why: N-acetylglutamate is an essential allosteric activator for Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase I (CPS I).

questions.stem: The major regulatory step in urea cycle is catalyzed by;
questions.why: CPS I catalyzes the committed, rate-limiting step of the urea cycle.

questions.stem: Ammonia generated in the body enters the urea cycle in which of the following forms?
questions.why: The two nitrogen atoms enter as ammonium (NH4+, via carbamoyl phosphate) and aspartate.

questions.stem: The glucose alanine cycle puts burden on the liver via gluconeogenesis. Which of the following acts as the acceptor of the amino group in the liver?
questions.why: In the liver, alanine transfers its amino group to α-ketoglutarate.

questions.stem: Which of the following amino acid: Keto acid pair bridges the urea cycle with the tricarboxylic acid cycle for the maintenance of the nitrogen and amino acid pool?
questions.why: Aspartate donates its amino group to the urea cycle and becomes oxaloacetate, which can enter the TCA cycle.

questions.stem: Urea cycle provides intermediate for which pathway?
questions.why: The urea cycle produces fumarate, which directly enters the TCA cycle.

questions.stem: Urea is formed from:
questions.why: The final step of the urea cycle is catalyzed by arginase, which cleaves arginine into urea and ornithine.

questions.stem: An essential amino acid in man is:
questions.why: Methionine cannot be synthesized by the human body and must be obtained from the diet.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is semi essential amino acid for humans?
questions.why: Arginine is conditionally essential; dietary intake is required during periods of rapid growth or stress.

questions.stem: An example of polar amino acid is:
questions.why: Arginine is a highly polar, positively charged (basic) amino acid.

questions.stem: The amino acid with a nonpolar side chain is:
questions.why: Valine contains a hydrophobic aliphatic side chain.

questions.stem: A ketogenic amino acid is:
questions.why: Isoleucine is broken down to acetyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA, so it is ketogenic (as well as glucogenic). Valine, cysteine and glycine are glucogenic only.

questions.stem: All the following are sulphur containing amino acids found in proteins except:
questions.why: Threonine has a hydroxyl group but does not contain sulfur.

questions.stem: An aromatic amino acid is:
questions.why: Tyrosine contains an aromatic benzene ring.

questions.stem: The principal end product of protein metabolism, which is excreted in the greatest quantity in human urine, is:
questions.why: Urea is the primary nitrogenous waste product of protein catabolism.

questions.stem: Glutamate decarboxylation results in formation of inhibitory transmitter in CNS. Name it.
questions.why: Glutamate decarboxylase removes CO2 from glutamate to synthesize Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA).

questions.stem:
Assertion: Transdeamination is a multi-step reaction to generate ammonia.
Reason: Transdeamination involves decarboxylation reaction followed by oxidative deamination.
questions.why: The assertion is true. The reason is false: transdeamination involves transamination followed by oxidative deamination.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Alanine-glucose cycle imposes the burden of gluconeogenesis on the liver.
Reason: Alanine-glucose cycle transports alanine from the muscle through the blood to the liver.
questions.why: Both true. The transport of alanine is the mechanism, not the reason why it's a burden.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Ureogenesis is an energy expensive process.
Reason: Ureogenesis utilizes two molecules of ATP.
questions.why: The assertion is true. The reason is false: the urea cycle consumes three ATP.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Urea cycle predominantly occurs in the mitochondria.
Reason: Urea cycle has four of its steps occurring in the mitochondria.
questions.why: Both false. The urea cycle occurs partly in mitochondria and partly in cytosol. Only two steps occur in mitochondria.

questions.stem:
The metabolic fate of oxaloacetate includes:
I. condensing with acetyl CoA and committing to TCA cycle
II. conversion to glucose
III. conversion to aspartate.
questions.why: Oxaloacetate can enter the TCA cycle, be converted to glucose, or be transaminated to aspartate.

questions.stem:
The generation of ammonia in the reaction catalysed by glutamate dehydrogenase:
I. requires the participation of NAD+ or NADP+
II. may be reversed to consume ammonia when present in excess
III. is enhanced by increased ATP/ADP or GTP/GDP.
questions.why: i is true. ii is true. iii is false; high ATP/GTP inhibits the enzyme.

questions.stem:
The accumulation of ammonia may lead to the following:
I. Impaired protein synthesis
II. Decreased synthesis of ATP
III. impaired impulse conduction.
questions.why: Ammonia depletes alpha-ketoglutarate, impairs protein synthesis, and alters neurotransmitters.

questions.stem:
The carbon skeleton of cysteine is metabolised to:
I. pyruvate
II. taurine
III. glutathione
questions.why: Cysteine is converted to pyruvate and taurine. Glutathione is a peptide formed from cysteine, not a carbon skeleton end-product.

questions.stem:
The components of folic acid are:
I. para-amino benzoic acid
II. substituted pteridine
III. glutamine.
questions.why: Folic acid consists of PABA and a pteridine ring. (It contains glutamate, not glutamine).

questions.stem:
The following groups of amino acids are purely glycogenic:
I. serine, alanine, threonine
II. aspartate, cysteine, histidine
III. isoleucine, asparagine, threonine.
questions.why: Serine, alanine, aspartate, cysteine, histidine are glycogenic. Threonine and isoleucine are both.

questions.stem:
The following amino acids are both glycogenic and ketogenic:
I. isoleucine
II. tyrosine
III. serine.
questions.why: Isoleucine and tyrosine are both. Serine is purely glycogenic.

questions.stem:
The carbon skeletons of the following amino acids are converted to acetyl CoA:
I. tyrosine
II. isoleucine
III. tryptophan.
questions.why: All three are ketogenic (or both) and yield acetyl CoA during degradation.

questions.stem:
Polar uncharged amino acids:
I. Serine
II. Cysteine
III. Methionine.
questions.why: Serine and cysteine have polar, uncharged side chains. Methionine's thioether side chain is hydrophobic, so it is classed as non-polar.

questions.stem:
The following are polar positively charged amino acids:
I. arginine
II. glutamine
III. glutamate.
questions.why: Arginine is basic (positive). Glutamine is polar uncharged. Glutamate is acidic (negative).

questions.stem:
Assertion: Unusual amino acids result from modifications of the common amino acids.
Reason: Unusual amino acids have no genetic coding for their biosynthesizing enzymes.
questions.why: The assertion is true (e.g., hydroxyproline). The reason is false: they are modified after translation, but the enzymes that modify them are genetically coded.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Glutamate dehydrogenase is an allosteric enzyme.
Reason: Glutamate dehydrogenase activity is activated by high levels of GTP and ADP.
questions.why: The assertion is true. The reason is false: it is activated by ADP and GDP, and inhibited by ATP and GTP.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Pyridoxal phosphate serves a prosthetic group in the transfer an amino group to an α-keto acid.
Reason: Pyridoxal phosphate serves as coenzyme tightly bound to transaminase.
questions.why: Both true. PLP acts as a tightly bound prosthetic group for transaminases to transfer amino groups.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Oxidative deamination reactions generate reducing equivalents for biosynthesis.
Reason: Oxidative deamination produces NADH as a byproduct.
questions.why: The reason is true: glutamate dehydrogenase uses NAD+ (or NADP+) and produces NADH when it deaminates glutamate. The assertion is false as stated: the NADH from oxidative deamination mainly feeds the electron transport chain for ATP, while biosynthesis uses NADPH, which glutamate dehydrogenase consumes in the reverse (reductive amination) direction.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate belongs to the hydrolases.
Reason: fructose 1,6-bisphosphate is involved in aldol cleavage.
questions.why: The assertion is false: fructose 1,6-bisphosphate is a substrate, not an enzyme (the enzyme that hydrolyses it, fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase, is the hydrolase). The reason is true: aldolase splits fructose 1,6-bisphosphate by aldol cleavage into DHAP and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Lysine is an essential amino acid.
Reason: lysine cannot be synthesized by the human body and must be obtained from the diet.
questions.why: Both statements are true, and the reason perfectly defines why lysine is essential.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Fructose is absorbed directly into the bloodstream.
Reason: fructose is one of the dietary monosaccharides.
questions.why: Both are true. Because it is a monosaccharide (already a simple sugar), it requires no digestion and is absorbed directly.

questions.stem:
The urea cycle:
I. synthesis of carbamoyl phosphate is enhanced by amino acid ingestion
II. ornithine transcarbamoylase is also active in the cytosol of humans
III. the generation of a mole of urea requires the expenditure of four high-energy phosphate bonds
questions.why: A protein meal raises N-acetylglutamate, which activates CPS I, so carbamoyl phosphate synthesis rises (I). Each urea costs 3 ATP but 4 high-energy bonds, because argininosuccinate synthetase splits ATP to AMP + PPi (III). Ornithine transcarbamoylase is mitochondrial only (II false).

questions.stem:
Ammonia is toxic because:
I. it inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase system
II. it reverses the glutamate dehydrogenase reaction
III. it impedes synthesis of the neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid
questions.why: Excess ammonia drives glutamate dehydrogenase backwards, draining α-ketoglutarate from the TCA cycle and cutting ATP production (II). It also diverts glutamate into glutamine, reducing GABA synthesis (III), and NH4+ competes with K+ at the Na+/K+-ATPase, disturbing neuronal membranes (I).

questions.stem:
Phenylketonuria:
I. the characteristic slight dilution of skin and hair pigmentation is due to a defective phenylalanine hydroxylase
II. may be characterized by high levels of phenylpyruvic acid in the urine of affected subjects
III. may be due to deficiency in tetrahydrobiopterin.
questions.why: All are true. Defective PAH causes pale skin, phenylpyruvate is excreted in urine, and BH4 is a required cofactor.

questions.stem: In a child's urine were detected phenylpyruvate and phenylacetate. What enzyme insufficiency causes this?
questions.why: Phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) deficiency causes Phenylketonuria (PKU).

questions.stem:
Which of these amino acids can result in maple syrup disease during catabolism of their carbon chain:
I. Leucine
II. Valine
III. isoleucine
questions.why: MSUD is caused by a defect in the branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex, affecting all three.

questions.stem:
Intermittent branch chain ketonuria is characterized by:
I. symptoms appearing early in life
II. variant of maple syrup urine disease
III. deficiency in α-keto dehydrogenase complex:
questions.why: It is a variant of MSUD (ii) caused by the enzyme deficiency (iii), but symptoms appear intermittently, often later.

questions.stem:
Tyrosinaemia is characterized by the following:
I. type III tyrosinaemia is associated with the deficiency of parahydroxy phenylpyruvate dioxygenase
II. type I tyrosinaemia is associated with increased susceptibility to hepatorenal disease and hepatic cancers
III. type II tyrosinaemia is associated with the deficiency of fumarylacetoaetase.
questions.why: i is true. ii is true. iii is false (Type II is due to tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency).

questions.stem:
Tyrosinaemia type II is associated with:
I. intellectual disability
II. eye and skin lesions
III. seizures.
questions.why: Tyrosinaemia type II (Richner–Hanhart syndrome, tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency) causes painful corneal lesions, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis (skin lesions) and intellectual disability in about half of patients. Seizures are not a characteristic feature.

questions.stem:
Deficiency of the following enzymes may be characterized by the following:
I. ornithine transcarbamylase and citrullinaemia
II. argininosuccinate lyase and argininosuccinic aciduria
III. carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and hyperammonaemia.
questions.why: Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency causes argininosuccinic aciduria, and CPS I deficiency causes hyperammonaemia. Statement I is false: ornithine transcarbamoylase deficiency causes hyperammonaemia with orotic aciduria; citrullinaemia comes from argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency.

questions.stem:
Cystathionuria is associated with the following:
I. reduced affinity of cystathionine y lyase
II. deficiency of biotin
III. deficiency of cystathionine β synthase.
questions.why: Cystathionuria is caused by a defect in cystathionine gamma-lyase (i).

questions.stem:
Homocystinuria is caused by:
I. methionine synthase
II. pyridoxal phosphate
III. deficiency of cystathionine β synthase.
questions.why: Defects in methionine synthase, lack of PLP, and CBS deficiency can all lead to homocystinuria.

questions.stem:
Isovaleryl acidemia is characterized by:
I. speech defects
II. it is associated with mild mental retardation
III. cheesy odour.
questions.why: Isovaleric acidemia causes speech defects, mild intellectual disability, and a distinct 'sweaty feet' odor.

questions.stem:
Inborn errors of metabolism:
I. maybe manifested early in life
II. maybe manifested later in life
III. dependent on external factors.
questions.why: IEMs can present early or later (depending on severity/exposure to triggers).

questions.stem:
The biochemical consequences of metabolic block involve:
I. Reduction in substrate concentration
II. Interference with feedback mechanism
III. Reduced formation of product.
questions.why: In a block, the substrate accumulates (not reduces). It interferes with feedback and reduces the product.

questions.stem:
Initial specimen for detection of inborn errors of metabolism:
I. red cell haemolysates
II. skin biopsies
III. urine.
questions.why: All can be used depending on the suspected disorder.

questions.stem:
Specimen for prenatal screening for inborn error of metabolism include:
I. Chorionic villus sample
II. Amniotic fluid
III. Liver biopsy.
questions.why: CVS and amniotic fluid are prenatal. Liver biopsy is postnatal.

questions.stem:
Neonatal screening for inborn error focuses on a disease:
I. Relatively common in the population
II. Treatable
III. Easily tested.
questions.why: Screening requires the disease to be common, treatable, and have an easy test.

questions.stem:
Late clinical findings of inborn errors of metabolism may include:
I. Failure to thrive
II. Persistent jaundice
III. Intellectual disability.
questions.why: All are common presentations.

questions.stem:
Routine laboratory investigations for inborn error of metabolism related acid-base disturbance:
I. Blood gases
II. Bicarbonate
III. Plasma ammonia.
questions.why: All are standard tests for metabolic disorders.

questions.stem:
Management of inborn errors of metabolism focuses on:
I. Limiting precursors in affected pathway
II. Reduce the accumulated products
III. Supply the deficient enzyme.
questions.why: All are valid strategies.

questions.stem:
Classic galactosaemia is as a result of a defect in the enzyme:
I. Galactokinase
II. UDP-galactose-4-epimerase
III. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase.
questions.why: Classic galactosemia is caused by GALT (uridyltransferase) deficiency.

questions.stem:
Precursor amino acids in the inborn error of metabolism methyl malonic aciduria:
I. Isoleucine
II. Leucine
III. Serine.
questions.why: Methylmalonic aciduria is caused by defects in the breakdown of isoleucine (and valine, methionine, threonine).

questions.stem:
These conditions are due to mutations in transport proteins:
I. Menkes syndrome
II. Cystinosis
III. Thalassaemia.
questions.why: Menkes (copper transport) and Cystinosis (cystine transport) are transporter defects.

questions.stem:
Inborn errors of metabolism caused by mutation in hormonal receptor genes:
I. Dwarfism
II. Vitamin D dependent ricket
III. Testicular feminization.
questions.why: All can result from receptor mutations.

questions.stem:
Assertion: PKU, MSUD and alkaptonuria are inheritable disease.
Reason: PKU, MSUD and alkaptonuria are caused by defects in protein metabolism.
questions.why: Both are true, but they are inheritable because of genetic mutations, not just because they affect metabolism.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Histidinaemia is associated with elevated blood, CSF and urinary excretion of histidine and its metabolites.
Reason: Histidinaemia is characterized by decreased concentration of urocanic acid in blood and skin.
questions.why: Both are true. In histidinaemia, histidase deficiency blocks histidine → urocanic acid, so histidine and its by-products rise in blood, CSF and urine, and urocanic acid falls in blood and skin. Low urocanic acid is a parallel consequence of the same block, not the cause of the high histidine.

questions.stem: A result of mutation in gene coding for the enzyme that catalysis a deamination process in haem synthesis.
questions.why: AIP is caused by deficiency of PBG deaminase.

questions.stem: Caused by mutation of protein involved in cellular growth control.
questions.why: Retinoblastoma is caused by mutations in the RB tumor suppressor gene.

questions.stem:
Tay Sachs disease presents with:
I. Muscle weakness
II. Patient presents with diminished muscle tone
III. Deterioration of cognitive processes.
questions.why: All are features of Tay-Sachs (developmental regression, hypotonia, weakness).

questions.stem:
In osteogenesis imperfecta:
I. The gene COL1A1 is implicated
II. Triple helix formation is slow
III. Cross-linking of protein fiber is compact.
questions.why: COL1A1 mutations cause defective collagen. Triple helix formation is slow/defective. Cross-linking is deficient, not compact.

questions.stem:
α-keto acid dehydrogenase complex is synonymous to:
I. pyruvate dehydrogenase complex
II. glutamate dehydrogenase
III. malate dehydrogenase.
questions.why: The alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex usually refers to the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.

questions.stem:
Phenylketonuria:
I. incidence of 1:100,000 live births
II. associated with light hair, eye and skin
III. an autosomal recessive condition.
questions.why: Incidence is closer to 1:10,000. It is autosomal recessive and causes pale pigmentation.

questions.stem: A hormonal (growth-factor receptor) defect.
questions.why: Achondroplasia is caused by an activating mutation of FGFR3, the receptor for fibroblast growth factor, a growth-signalling defect. Retinoblastoma is a tumour-suppressor (growth control) defect, retinitis pigmentosa a photoreceptor defect, AIP an enzyme defect and cystinosis a transporter defect.

questions.stem: Involves a defect in a light-sensitive receptor.
questions.why: Many cases of retinitis pigmentosa are caused by mutations in rhodopsin, the light-sensitive receptor of rod cells, leading to progressive loss of photoreceptors.

questions.why: Porphin is a macrocyclic ring structure.

options.label: A

questions.why: PCT patients present with cutaneous photosensitivity.

questions.stem: The following is true about the formation of haem:

options.label: A
options.text: six moles of porphobilinogen react to form a linear hexapyrrole

options.label: B
options.text: four moles of porphobilinogen react to form uroporphyrinogen III under the action of porphobilinogen deaminase

options.label: C
options.text: uroporphyrinogen III co-synthase isomerises uroporphyrinogen I to uroporphyrinogen III

options.label: D

questions.why: Four molecules of PBG condense to form a linear tetrapyrrole which cyclizes to uroporphyrinogen I, then III.

questions.stem: The following enzymes in haem synthesis are properly matched with their actions;

options.label: A
options.text: uroporphyrinogen (UPG) I synthase: condensation of 6 moles of porphobilinogen

options.label: B
options.text: porphobilinogen deaminase: synthesis of uroporphyrinogen III

options.label: C
options.text: uroporphyrinogen III decarboxylase: decarboxylation of the acetate side chains in uroporphyrinogen III

The condensation uses 4 (not 6) PBG, PBG deaminase alone gives the linear hydroxymethylbilane (UPG III needs the co-synthase), and protoporphyrinogen IX is oxidised by protoporphyrinogen oxidase.

questions.stem:
The allosteric manifestations of haemoglobin include:
I. Co-operative binding of O2
II. The sigmoidal nature of the haemoglobin oxygen dissociation curve
III. Conformational changes in structure brought about by a lowering of pH
questions.why: All three are key allosteric properties (Bohr effect for pH).

questions.stem:
The oxygen dissociation curves for myoglobin and haemoglobin show that:
I. Myoglobin is more saturated with oxygen at any given PO2
II. The myoglobin curve always lies to the right of the haemoglobin curve
III. The haemoglobin curve has a sigmoid shape
questions.why: The myoglobin curve lies to the left.

III. buffering of H+ ions

questions.stem:
The following statements are true about myoglobin:
I. The first amino acid in helix A is designated A1, the second A2, and so forth.
II. The molecule has altogether 7 non-helical segments.
III. The N-terminal non-helical region is made up of two amino acid residues designated N1 and N2.
questions.why: Helix residues are numbered by helix letter and position (A1, A2 …), so I is true. The terminal non-helical residues are designated NA1 and NA2 (and HC1–HC5 at the C-terminus), not N1 and N2, so III is false. II is also false.

questions.stem:
In myoglobin:
I. The N-terminal non-helical region is made up of two amino acid residues designated NA1 and NA2
II. The oxygen binding site is the sixth co-ordination position of the haem iron
III. The carboxyl terminal non-helical region comprises five amino acids termed H1 through to H5.
questions.why: The C-terminal region is designated HC1-HC5, not H1-H5.

questions.stem:
The following is true about the distribution of amino-acids in myoglobin:
I. The interior of myoglobin consists entirely of non-polar amino-acids
II. The interior of myoglobin has only two polar amino-acids
III. The interior of myoglobin consists of residues such as leucine, valine, methionine and phenylalanine.
questions.why: The interior is packed with hydrophobic residues such as leucine, valine, methionine and phenylalanine (III). It is almost, but not entirely, non-polar (I is false): the only polar residues inside are the two histidines (E7 and F8) at the haem pocket (II).

questions.stem:
Concerning amino acid distribution in myoglobin:
I. Side chains of glutamate, aspartate, glutamine, asparagine, lysine or arginine are abundant in the interior of myoglobin.
II. Residues that have both a polar and a non-polar part, such as threonine, tyrosine, and tryptophan are positioned such that their non-polar part points inward.
III. Only two polar residues are found in the interior of myoglobin
questions.why: Charged and polar side chains (Glu, Asp, Gln, Asn, Lys, Arg) are on the surface, so I is false. Amphipathic residues such as Thr, Tyr and Trp point their non-polar parts inward (II), and the only polar residues in the interior are the two histidines E7 and F8 (III).

questions.stem:
Interactions at the active site of haemoglobin:
I. The distal histidine and other residues surrounding the sixth co-ordination point block the formation of haem-oxygen-haem sandwiches
II. Amino acids surrounding the sixth co-ordination point stabilize the ferrous form of myoglobin.
III. The polypeptide chain in haemoglobin creates a hindered haem environment
questions.why: All are true features of the globin pocket.

questions.stem:
The following statements are true:
I. The affinity of free haem for carbon monoxide and oxygen is about the same
II. In myoglobin and haemoglobin, the binding affinity for CO is 200 times that of O2.
III. The hindered haem environment ensures a reduction in affinity for carbon monoxide and reversible binding of oxygen
questions.why: In myoglobin and haemoglobin, CO binds about 200 times more tightly than O2 (II). That is far less than free haem, which binds CO about 25 000 times more strongly than O2 (so I is false). The hindered pocket (distal histidine forcing a bent geometry) cuts CO affinity and lets O2 bind reversibly (III).

questions.stem:
An active site in haemoglobin:
I. Has histidine F8 attached
II. Has histidine E7 attached
III. Can bind CO2, O2 and CO
questions.why: The proximal histidine F8 is bonded to the haem iron (I). The distal histidine E7 sits near the sixth position but is not attached (II false). The haem site binds O2 and CO, but CO2 binds to the N-terminal amino groups of the globin chains, not the haem (III false).

questions.stem:
A haemoglobin active site:
I. Is modulated by histidine E7 and other surrounding amino acid side chains
II. Is not affected by binding of O2 to another binding site
III. Binds 2,3 BPG as it off loads O2
questions.why: The haem site is modulated by the distal histidine E7 and surrounding residues (I). It is affected by O2 binding at the other subunits (cooperativity), so II is false. 2,3-BPG binds in the central cavity between the β chains, not at the active site, so III is false.

questions.stem:
Haemoglobin S:
I. has a substitution of glutamic acid for valine at position 6 on the β chain
II. has a sticky patch on its surface even when fully oxygenated
III. when deoxygenated has complementary sites that can accommodate the sticky patches
questions.why: In HbS, valine replaces glutamate at position 6 of the β chain (the item's wording 'substitution of glutamic acid for valine' is the lecturer's phrasing for this change). Val-6 forms a hydrophobic 'sticky patch' that is present in both oxy- and deoxy-HbS, but the complementary pocket it fits into appears only on deoxy-HbS, so polymers form when HbS is deoxygenated.

questions.stem:
Concerning haemoglobin S:
I. the sickling of HbS is reversible
II. even when fully oxygenated has complementary sites that can accommodate the sticky patches created by valine at position 6 on the β chain
III. polymerizes by the interaction of sticky patches with complementary sites
questions.why: HbS polymerises when the Val-6 sticky patch of one molecule fits into the complementary site of another (III). Fully oxygenated HbS has no complementary sites (II false). Repeated sickling eventually becomes irreversible, which is why the item treats I as false.

questions.stem:

I. more than 50% of the haemoglobin in the red blood cells is HbS
II. some of the red blood cells have HbA molecules only while other red blood cells carry HbS molecules only
III. both HbS and HbA molecules are present in all the red blood cells
questions.why: Trait has ~40% HbS. Both HbA and HbS are in every RBC.

questions.stem:

I. Normally no HbF is detected
II. The concentration of HbS is too low for sickling to occur at normal oxygen levels
III. Deoxygenation of the tissues can trigger off a sickling crisis
questions.why: HbF is often detected in small amounts. Deoxygenation triggers sickling.

questions.stem:

I. Sickle cell SC disease
II. Sickle cell S-Thalassaemia
III. Sickle cell SS disease
questions.why: Strictly, sickle cell anaemia means the homozygous SS genotype. SC disease and S/β-thalassaemia are other forms of sickle cell DISEASE, not sickle cell anaemia.

questions.why: They inhibit formation and mimic the C-terminal sequence. They do not dissolve formed crystals.

questions.why: They act as decoys by mimicking the complementary site, not the sticky patch.

questions.why: Thalassemias are quantitative defects (reduced production), not qualitative structural defects.
